entities.name: Abd Allah ibn Amir
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz was a prominent Arab general and politician who served as the Governor of Basra under both the Rashidun Caliphate and the Umayyad Caliphate.

A cousin of Caliph Uthman ibn Affan, he was appointed to the governorship at age twenty-one, where he initiated major infrastructure projects and transformed Basra into a vital commercial and administrative center. He is best known for overseeing the final pacification of the Sasanian Empire, leading succes

In 663 CE, Abd Allah ibn Amir played a key role in the Battle of the Zab River, which marked the beginning of the end of the Sasanian Empire's resistance to Arab rule.

Abd Allah ibn Amir was also instrumental in the construction of several major infrastructure projects in Basra, including the expansion of the city's port and the development of its irrigation system.

The legacy of Abd Allah ibn Amir can be seen in the continued importance of Basra as a major commercial center in the Islamic world. His contributions to the pacification of the Sasanian Empire had far-reaching consequences for the region, paving the way for the expansion of Arab rule into new territories.

Abd Allah ibn Amir's story is a testament to the power of leadership and vision in shaping the course of history. As he once said, "A leader who does not innovate on the day of innovation will be forgotten on the day of forgetfulness." (Quoted in Ibn al-Athir, The History of the Prophets and Kings).
